title: Pneumonia Associated with Oxygenation Strategies for Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure in Adults
author: Satoshi Hokari
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bup5nvq6
materials: which the studies were conducted were restricted to English and Japanese. Randomized crossover trials, cluster-randomized trials, and quasi-experimental trials were excluded. Condition or domain being studied Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure is organ failure that is frequently observed in critically ill patients. While ventilation management by endo tracheal intubation is a reliable method of respiratory support, IMV has been associated with various adverse events. Avoiding endotracheal intubation and noninvasive oxygenation strategies such as NPPV or HFNC can reduce severe complications and improve o utcomes in respiratory failure management. On the other hand, patients treated with NPPV may have a potential risk of aspiration pneumonia compared with no ventilation. Furthermore, whether noninvasive oxygenation devices, NPPV or HFNC, have more favorable effects for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure patients have not been thoroughly investigated. Few studies have investigated the risk of pneumonia associated with noninvasive oxygenation strategies and compared these two devices in patients with acute hy poxemic respiratory failure. Type of participants Inclusion: We will include patients aged 18 years or older who have acute respiratory failure, defined by the new onset (<7 days) of clinical signs (e.g., tachypnea, increased work of breathing), radiologic signs (unilateral or bilateral chest X-ray opacities), and hypoxemia. Hypoxemia was defined as a P/F ratio below 300 cm H2O, SaO2/SpO2 <94% in room air, PaO2 <60 mmHg with room air, or <80 mmHg with O2. We will utilize studies that include patients treated in the intensive care unit, intermediate care unit, and emergency department. Exclusion: 1) Hypercapnia (e.g., >50 mmHg) in more than 50% of the study’s population 2) Patients with congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or asthma as the cause of respiratory failure, and more than 50% of the study population 3) Post-extubation respiratory failure (>50% population) 4) Post-surgical patients (>50% population) 5) Post-trauma patients (>50% population) 6) The absence of informed consent 7) Do-not-resuscitate orders 8) Intervention is limited in the emergency department or pre-hospital care

steps.title: Screen and Extract Study Data
steps.instruction: Two of three physicians (HO, SK, SH) independently screen titles, abstracts, and full texts to identify relevant studies and extract data into standardized forms.

substeps.instruction: Perform first screening of titles and abstracts.
Perform second screening of full texts.

Extract study characteristics: methods (design, duration, centers, setting, withdrawals, date), participants (N, mean age, age range, sex, severity, diagnostic/inclusion/exclusion criteria), interventions (method and comparison), and outcomes (primary/secondary and time points).
Resolve disagreements via discussion with the third physician or by contacting original authors if abstracts are insufficient.
Copy extracted data from collection forms into Review Manager (RevMan) 5 by one review author (MS).

steps.title: Assess Risk of Bias
steps.instruction: Two of three review authors (HO, SK, SH) independently assess the risk of bias for primary and secondary outcomes using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0.

substeps.instruction: Evaluate the following seven domains: (a) random sequence generation, (b) allocation concealment, (c) blinding of participants and personnel, (d) blinding of outcome assessors, (e) incomplete outcome data, (f) selective outcome reporting, and (g) other sources of bias.
Grade each bias as 'low-risk', 'unclear-risk', or 'high-risk' (or 'some concerns' for specific domains).
Resolve discrepancies through discussion with the third reviewer as necessary.

steps.title: Perform Data Synthesis and Meta-Analysis
steps.instruction: Synthesize data using RevMan 5.3 (2014) to calculate effect sizes and pool outcomes.

substeps.instruction: Calculate relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) for categorical data.
Calculate weighted mean differences with 95% CI for continuous data.
Pool outcome measures using a random effect model.
Set significance threshold at a two-sided p-value < 0.05.

steps.title: Assess Heterogeneity
steps.instruction: Evaluate study heterogeneity between trials for each outcome.

substeps.instruction: Perform visual inspection of forest plots.
Quantify inconsistency using the I² statistic (0-40%: might not be important; 30-60%: moderate; 50-90%: substantial; 75-100%: considerable).
Investigate reasons for heterogeneity if I² > 50% using the χ² test (p-value).

steps.title: Conduct Network Meta-Analysis
steps.instruction: Perform a network meta-analysis using a frequentist-based approach with multivariate random effects meta-analysis, following the GRADE Working Group Approach.

substeps.instruction: Estimate network model inconsistency using inconsistency factors and their uncertainty.
Construct ranking plots (rankograms) based on the probability of a treatment having the highest event rate.
Use the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) to establish the treatment hierarchy.

description: Background Noninvasive oxygenation strategies, such as noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV) and high -flow nasal cannula (HFNC), have become common treatments for acute respiratory failure (ARF). Compared with invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), NPPV reduces hospital stay, morbidity, and mortality in patients with ARF1. Recently, using a systemic review and network meta-analysis approach, Ferreyro BL et al. have reported that treatment with noninvasive oxygenation strategies was associated with a lower risk of death than standard oxygen therapy in adult patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure2. However, further research is needed to understand the relative benefits and risks of each strategy. While NPPV reduces the risk of pneumonia associated with IMV , aspiration pneumonia has been described in as many as 5% of NPPV patients3, suggesting a potential risk of pneumonia associated with NPPV . Consistently, Kohlenberg et al. reported that NPPV might increase pneumonia risk compared with no ventilation, according to the nosocomial infection surveillance system database 4. In contrast, previous investigations have reported a lower incidence of pne umonia with NPPV than with no ventilation 5. Therefore, the risk of pneumonia associated with NPPV remains controversial. In addition, noninvasive oxygenation devices, NPPV or HFNC, having more favorable effec ts for patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure have not been thoroughly investigated. Frat et al. reported a lower mortality rate in the group treated with HFNC than the group treated with standard oxygen therapy or NPPV in a randomized clinical trial6. However, the differences among the noninvasive oxygenation intervention outcomes remain unclear. Review question Which noninvasive oxygenation strategy is best for reducing pneumonia in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure?
